title: Ivory, Flutes and Painted Lions
subtitle: The Aurignacian and Europe’s first figurative art
summary: In the Swabian Jura and at Chauvet, Europe’s early Homo sapiens carved ivory animals and a lion-headed figure, played bone and ivory flutes and painted lions and rhinos by firelight. Discoveries in Sulawesi now show that such art was not a European invention.
narration: In September 2008, in the Hohle Fels cave in southwest Germany, Nicholas Conard’s team lifted six fragments of mammoth ivory from the lowest Upper Palaeolithic layer. Fitted together, they formed a woman six centimetres tall, with huge breasts, a carefully carved pubic triangle and, instead of a head, a small ring for hanging on a cord. She is at least 40,000 years old.

As the Neanderthals faded, the newcomers to Europe made art of a kind never seen there before. In the valleys of the Swabian Jura they carved horses, mammoths, cave lions and a human figure with a lion’s head, and they played flutes made from the wing bones of vultures and swans and from hollowed ivory, the oldest known musical instruments. Archaeologists call their culture the Aurignacian, after a cave at Aurignac in the French Pyrenees foothills.

A few thousand years later, on the walls of Chauvet Cave in southern France, artists drew prides of lions, charging rhinoceroses and herds of horses with a confidence that astonished everyone when the cave was found in 1994. For a century such art was taken as proof of a creative explosion unique to Europe. Painted animals in Sulawesi, older still, have ended that idea. What remains open is what the images meant to the people who made them.

body.heading: The Swabian Jura: the oldest figurines
paragraphs: Caves in two small valleys of southwest Germany, the Ach and the Lone, have produced several dozen ivory figurines from Aurignacian layers dated by radiocarbon to between about 43,000 and 35,000 years ago. In 2017 six of these caves were inscribed together as the UNESCO World Heritage Site “Caves and Ice Age Art in the Swabian Jura”.

At Vogelherd, excavated by Gustav Riek in 1931, the finds included a small horse, mammoths and lions; in 2006 Nicholas Conard’s team, sieving the old spoil heaps, found a complete little mammoth. At Hohlenstein-Stadel in 1939, Robert Wetzel and Otto Völzing recovered hundreds of ivory fragments that were recognised as a figure only three decades later. Reassembled by Joachim Hahn in 1969 and again in 2012–2013 with newly excavated pieces, the Lion Man (Löwenmensch) stands 31.1 centimetres tall: an upright body with a cave lion’s head, carved from a mammoth tusk about 40,000 years ago. Experimental carving by Wulf Hein suggests it took hundreds of hours of skilled work.

The Hohle Fels figure, published by Conard in Nature in 2009, is the oldest undisputed depiction of a human body. The first report gave a minimum age of 35,000 years; later radiocarbon work on the basal Aurignacian there places it at about 40,000 years or more.

body.heading: The first music
paragraphs: In the same layer at Hohle Fels, excavators found a nearly complete flute made from the wing bone of a griffon vulture, 21.8 centimetres long with five finger holes, along with fragments of ivory flutes. Geißenklösterle produced flutes of swan bone and of mammoth ivory; making an ivory flute meant splitting a curved piece of tusk, hollowing both halves and fitting them back together airtight. Radiocarbon dating by Tom Higham, Nicholas Conard and colleagues in 2012 placed the start of the Aurignacian at Geißenklösterle at about 43,000–42,000 years ago. Replicas play a range of notes, and music, presumably with song and dance, was part of life from the beginning of the Upper Palaeolithic.

body.heading: Chauvet
paragraphs: On 18 December 1994 three cavers, Jean-Marie Chauvet, Éliette Brunel and Christian Hillaire, entered a sealed cave above the Ardèche gorge near Vallon-Pont-d’Arc. Inside were hundreds of animal images, among them horses, aurochs, bison, reindeer and cave bears, but above all animals rarely painted elsewhere: cave lions, woolly rhinoceroses and mammoths. The artists shaded with charcoal, scraped walls white before drawing, used bulges in the rock to give bodies volume and repeated outlines to suggest movement. A hanging rock bears the lower body of a woman merged with a bison.

The first radiocarbon dates, on charcoal from the drawings themselves, were far older than style suggested. Christian Züchner, and Paul Pettitt with Paul Bahn, argued that such mastery belonged later, in the Gravettian or Solutrean, and that the samples might be contaminated. The answer came from sheer weight of evidence. In 2016 Anita Quiles, Jean-Michel Geneste and colleagues combined 259 radiocarbon dates on charcoal, bones and drawings into a model with two phases of activity, about 37,000–33,500 and 31,000–28,000 years ago, while cosmogenic chlorine-36 dating by Benjamin Sadier and colleagues (2012) showed that rockfalls had closed the entrance by about 21,000 years ago. Chauvet was inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2014; visitors see a full-scale replica.

body.heading: Fumane and El Castillo
paragraphs: At Grotta di Fumane in the Lessini hills north of Verona, stones that fell from the cave roof into Aurignacian layers of around 40,000 years ago carry red ochre paintings, including an animal and a figure with horn-like projections sometimes called the ‘shaman’. The same layers hold hundreds of perforated marine shells carried from the coast. Fumane’s older Neanderthal layers contain bird bones cut to remove large feathers, a hint that Neanderthals too decorated their bodies.

In northern Spain, Alistair Pike and colleagues in 2012 dated calcite crusts over paintings in eleven caves by the uranium-series method. A red disk in El Castillo came out at a minimum of 40,800 years and a hand stencil there at least 37,300. That is at or before the arrival of Homo sapiens in Cantabria, so the authors raised the possibility of Neanderthal painters. In 2018 Dirk Hoffmann and colleagues reported minimum ages above 64,000 years for a ladder-like red sign at La Pasiega, a hand stencil at Maltravieso and red-painted flowstone at Ardales, which would make them Neanderthal work.

body.heading: Beads, points and early genomes
paragraphs: The Aurignacian toolkit, with blades, thick ‘carinated’ pieces that served as cores for tiny bladelets, and split-based points of antler, spread across Europe between about 43,000 and 35,000 years ago. Its makers wore ornaments in quantity: pierced teeth, shells and ivory beads. Randall White has shown that basket-shaped ivory beads from southwest France were made in standardised stages, and shells travelled hundreds of kilometres inland. In 2006 Marian Vanhaeren and Francesco d’Errico mapped regional bead styles that may reflect distinct social or linguistic groups.

Genomes show who these people were. Kostenki 14 from the Don in Russia, about 37,000 years old, already belonged to the western Eurasian branch, separate from East Asians (Seguin-Orlando and colleagues, 2014). An individual from Goyet in Belgium, about 35,000 years old, carries ancestry that resurfaced in western Europe after the Ice Age, and a woman from Peștera Muierii in Romania, of similar age, shows high genetic diversity. The earlier pioneers of Bacho Kiro and Oase contributed little to any of them.

body.heading: What was the art for?
paragraphs: Interpretations have followed the intellectual fashions of their times. Around 1900 Salomon Reinach and the Abbé Henri Breuil read cave art as hunting magic: painting an animal, sometimes pierced by spears, would ensure success in the hunt. Yet in many caves the animals painted are not those most eaten, and at Chauvet predators dominate.

In the 1960s André Leroi-Gourhan and Annette Laming-Emperaire proposed a structuralist reading: decorated caves were organised spaces in which horses and bison, linked to male and female principles, formed the central pairing, with other animals at the margins. The scheme was influential but rested on Leroi-Gourhan’s own classifications and fits poorly with later, fully recorded caves such as Chauvet.

From the 1980s David Lewis-Williams, later joined by Jean Clottes, argued that much cave imagery drew on altered states of consciousness reached through dance, rhythm or sensory deprivation: geometric signs resemble the patterns people see in early trance, and composite figures such as the Lion Man reflect experiences of transformation in shamanic ritual. Critics including Paul Bahn and Patricia Helvenston object that ‘shamanism’ is defined too loosely, that the neuropsychological model is hard to test, and that it transplants southern African ethnography onto Ice Age Europe.

Other approaches look at context. Iegor Reznikoff and later acoustic surveys found that images cluster where caves resonate or echo. Hand stencils and finger flutings show that children, some very young, took part. Many researchers see the images as ways of storing and passing on knowledge of animals, seasons and territories; a 2023 proposal by Bennett Bacon and colleagues that dots and lines beside animals record a seasonal calendar remains contested. Most accept that no single explanation fits 30,000 years of art across a continent.

body.heading: Not a European miracle
paragraphs: For much of the twentieth century Aurignacian art was treated as evidence of a sudden ‘creative explosion’ in Europe about 40,000 years ago. Indonesia changed that. In 2014 Maxime Aubert and colleagues dated a hand stencil in Maros, Sulawesi, to at least 39,900 years and a painted babirusa to at least 35,400; later work in Borneo (at least 40,000 years) and Sulawesi pushed painted animals back to at least 45,500 years, a narrative scene to 51,200 and a hand stencil on Muna to 67,800 (chapter 19). Together with engraved ochre and shell beads in Africa more than 70,000 years old, these finds suggest that the capacity for art travelled with Homo sapiens out of Africa, and that where it survives depends largely on where rock and climate preserved it.

debates.question: Did Neanderthals paint in the caves of Spain?

views.label: Yes
views.text: Dirk Hoffmann, Alistair Pike, João Zilhão and colleagues argue that uranium-series minimum ages of more than 64,000 years at La Pasiega, Maltravieso and Ardales, long before Homo sapiens reached Iberia, can only mean Neanderthal artists, consistent with Neanderthal use of pigments, shells and feathers.

views.label: Not proven
views.text: Maxime Aubert, Adam Brumm and Jillian Huntley (2018), and separately Randall White and colleagues (2020), argue that uranium can leach from thin crusts, making them look too old; that some samples may not overlie deliberate marks; and that the ‘art’ is non-figurative red pigment whose human origin is uncertain in places.

debates.status: Open. The Ardales pigments are widely accepted as deliberate, but whether the dates are reliable and whether all the marks are Neanderthal work is still argued. Repeat sampling by independent labs and new dating methods such as laser-ablation uranium-series mapping may resolve it.

debates.question: Was Chauvet really painted more than 30,000 years ago?

views.label: Aurignacian and Gravettian phases
views.text: Jean Clottes, Jean-Michel Geneste, Anita Quiles and colleagues point to hundreds of consistent radiocarbon dates on drawings, torch marks and bones, and to rockfalls that sealed the cave by about 21,000 years ago.

views.label: Later, on stylistic grounds
views.text: Christian Züchner, Paul Pettitt and Paul Bahn argued in the late 1990s and 2000s that the refined style matched later art and that samples could have been contaminated or that artists used old charcoal.

debates.status: Resolved for most researchers since the 2016 chronological model: the first phase is about 37,000–33,500 years old. The lesson is that ‘primitive’ style is not a guide to age.

debates.question: What did Palaeolithic art mean?

views.label: Hunting magic
views.text: Salomon Reinach and Henri Breuil saw images as spells to secure prey; animals marked with spear-like lines seemed to support this.

views.label: Structural order
views.text: André Leroi-Gourhan saw a mythic system of paired animals and signs arranged by cave topography.

views.label: Shamanism and altered states
views.text: David Lewis-Williams and Jean Clottes relate signs and composite beings to trance experience and ritual journeys into the underworld.

views.label: Social information and experience
views.text: Others emphasise communication of knowledge, group identity, acoustics and the participation of children and whole communities.

debates.status: No single theory dominates. Most researchers now study particular caves and objects in context, and accept that meanings varied across tens of thousands of years and hundreds of communities.

keyFacts.label: Oldest figurative carvings
keyFacts.value: Swabian Jura ivories, about 40,000 years or more

keyFacts.label: Oldest musical instruments
keyFacts.value: Bird-bone and ivory flutes, about 43,000–40,000 years

sites.name: Hohle Fels
sites.summary: Cave near Schelklingen that yielded the oldest known figure of a human body, the ‘Venus’ of Hohle Fels, and a vulture-bone flute with five finger holes.

sites.name: Hohlenstein-Stadel
sites.summary: Cave in the Lone valley where the fragments of the Lion Man, a 31-centimetre ivory figure with a lion’s head, were found in 1939 and reassembled decades later.

sites.name: Vogelherd
sites.summary: Small cave that has produced the largest group of Aurignacian ivory animal figurines, including a horse, mammoths and lions.

sites.name: Geißenklösterle
sites.summary: Cave in the Ach valley with flutes of swan bone and mammoth ivory and some of the earliest radiocarbon dates for the Aurignacian.

sites.name: Chauvet-Pont d’Arc Cave
sites.summary: Cave discovered in 1994 with hundreds of animal images, including lions, rhinoceroses and mammoths, dated by more than 250 radiocarbon determinations.

sites.name: Grotta di Fumane
sites.summary: Cave in the Lessini hills with painted Aurignacian stones, hundreds of shell beads and earlier Neanderthal layers with evidence of feather removal.

sites.name: El Castillo
sites.summary: Cantabrian cave whose red disk, dated by uranium-series to at least 40,800 years, is among the oldest cave paintings in Europe and a candidate for Neanderthal authorship.

sites.name: Kostenki (Kostenki 14, Markina Gora)
sites.summary: Cluster of Upper Palaeolithic sites on the Don. The skeleton Kostenki 14 yielded one of the oldest European genomes, already on the western Eurasian branch.

sites.name: Goyet Caves
sites.summary: Caves in the Samson valley whose Aurignacian-age individual Goyet Q116-1 carries ancestry that reappears in Europe after the Last Glacial Maximum.

sites.name: Peștera Muierii
sites.summary: “Cave of the Women” in the southern Carpathians; the genome of a woman found here shows high diversity in Europe before the Ice Age maximum.
